name: Daria Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without ties to AI companies, employers or government. Your answers stay confidential. What fills an ordinary day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43, studied music at university and have taught clarinet for years. I play weddings with a quartet, record practice tracks and teach six pupils; reading new parts is normal work for me, though the fees are low.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is good about it, and what weighs on home life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A child finally finding a warm low note is the best part. My partner works catering hours that move with events, and our two children and mortgage leave less than one month of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the wedding quartet AI Plateau might speed the booking emails, but the couple still hires four people to play in the room. My clarinet pupils would keep their usual lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have played and taught for years, but low fees leave us with less than one month of bills saved. My partner’s catering hours move with events, so the mortgage worries me before any AI news does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the six clarinet pupils and the two signed weddings this season. Starting this month, I’d borrow the music stand from the community hall rather than replace mine, and use the saved cash for the electricity arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our household money even if the work itself stays familiar. One cancelled wedding would put the mortgage and power bill in the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a cancelled wedding remove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wedding deposit covers one grocery week, so I insist it be paid before we rehearse special music. I cannot pay the quartet from a couple’s good intentions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI now and then to sort the lesson calendar, not to hear whether a pupil breathes between phrases. A booking email cannot hear a cracked clarinet note.

say: I’d tell couples the **quartet** still needs four players in the room.
I would welcome faster **booking emails** while keeping deposits in writing.
think: My partner’s shifting **catering hours** and low music fees leave less than a month saved.
A cancelled **wedding** could put the mortgage and power bill in the same week.
do: Keep six **clarinet pupils** and two signed wedding dates this season.
Borrow a **music stand** from the hall instead of buying one while electricity arrears remain.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the mortgage despite little AI change.
fieldNote: Her mid-level **experience** protects the playing, but thin savings make ordinary cancellations serious.
She uses AI **occasionally** for the calendar and relies on paid deposits.
S0.quote: I cannot pay the quartet from a couple’s good intentions.

steps.text: Keep six clarinet pupils and two signed wedding dates
Borrow hall music stand instead of buying while power arrears remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the quartet Steady Disruption could remove the short clarinet recordings and the booking work before it replaces live players. I would ask the studio to show us paid dates, not a promise of future calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recorded teaching tracks make about a quarter of my income. I am competent at the instrument, but a cheap generated practice track could cost less than my afternoon, and our savings would not cover a long cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio this week for the next term’s paid recording list. If two track days disappear in the first year, I’d ask the hall for one extra beginner group only if a room is open, five families pay enough to cover hire and my time, and my partner can collect the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed if a quarter of my pay went while the electricity arrears stayed. A class without paying families is only another expense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the group pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five paid places cover the hall and my evening at the current rate. I would cancel the extra clarinet group if only four families signed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would collect the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner could collect the children after a catering shift, but only once the rota is confirmed. I would not advertise an evening class before we know who is home.

say: I’d ask for written **paid studio dates** as short recordings move to software.
I’d tell the quartet **live weddings** still need a separate fee agreement.
think: Practice tracks make about a **quarter** of my income and may become cheaper to generate.
Our thin **reserve** cannot carry a long recording cut.
do: Ask the **studio** this week for next term’s paid track dates.
Add a **clarinet group** in the first year after two lost track days only with an open room and five paying families.
Confirm **pickup** and fees covering hire and teaching time before advertising the group.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing a quarter of my pay while power arrears remain.
fieldNote: Her recorded **practice tracks** are exposed early, despite years of live and teaching experience.
The extra **group** needs five paid places, an open room and confirmed childcare before she advertises it.
S1.quote: A class without paying families is only another expense.

steps.text: Ask studio for written next-term paid recording dates
Add clarinet group first year after two lost days only with room and five paid families
Confirm partner pickup and five fees cover room and teaching time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our quartet AGI by 2028 could make lesson plans, practice tracks and booking cheap almost at once. Capable robots for hands-on playing would follow around 2031, so live weddings face a later deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the studio to stop buying my practice tracks in 2028, and some parents may switch to AI lessons. My partner’s catering work is uneven, and less than one month saved would not carry our mortgage through both losses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio now for written paid dates and the hall for next term’s pupil list. If recordings end in the first year after 2028, I’d drop the rented recording booth at renewal, keep my six pupils and ask the lender about a payment plan before arrears only if the household cash falls short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed because the lost tracks pay more than a small bill. Our mortgage would be due during the 2028 studio silence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How soon could you leave the booth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booth agreement has a notice period, so I would leave at renewal rather than pay a penalty. I could record nothing there if the studio stops ordering tracks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept lender relief?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lender for the total interest cost before agreeing to any relief. A smaller payment now could leave our children a bigger debt later.

say: I’d warn that **2028 thinking AGI** reaches tracks and plans before capable robots around 2031.
I would protect the quartet’s **signed weddings** while live playing still pays.
think: I expect **practice-track orders** to stop quickly, and some parents may leave lessons.
Our **thin reserve** and uneven catering pay cannot replace both sources.
do: Get written **studio dates** and the hall’s next pupil list now.
Leave the rented **recording booth** at renewal if orders end after 2028; keep six pupils.
Seek **lender terms** if cash falls short after 2028; review full written interest cost with partner before agreeing.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about lost tracks and the mortgage before robot players arrive.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 recorded work** from capable robots for live playing around 2031.
Booth cancellation respects **notice terms**; lender help requires a cash shortfall and full interest cost.
S2.quote: Our mortgage would be due during the 2028 studio silence.

steps.text: Get studio paid dates and hall pupil list now
Leave rented recording booth at renewal if orders end after 2028
Review full written interest with partner before lender relief if cash falls short after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the hall AGI by 2031 gives five years to see whether families still buy real clarinet lessons. Capable robots for hands-on playing follow around 2034, so the wedding quartet would have a little longer to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a music degree and years of lessons behind me, but I am not licensed to teach at a school. A funded teaching credential could help only if local schools accept it and I do not lose paid lessons while studying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask two schools this winter what credential they accept for a posted music-teacher role and ask the college whether a grant covers fees. I’d enroll only if the course misses no paid lessons and my partner can cover pickup; in the first year after 2031 I’d apply only if qualified and a posted wage covers travel, mortgage and childcare, keeping current pupils until a real offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the studio side, but five years gives me room to check the rules before spending. A degree in music is useful, yet it is not a school teaching license.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before enrolment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the school for the exact qualification on its job notice. I would not borrow for a course that the school does not accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could cover course nights?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner’s catering rota changes weekly, so childcare has to be checked for each course night. If the shift does not fit, I would wait for the next intake rather than miss paid lessons.

say: I’d ask schools about an **accepted credential** before taking a funded course.
I’d tell the quartet **2031 thinking AGI** precedes capable robot players around 2034.
think: My music **degree** does not itself qualify me for a school teaching post.
Tuition or lost **paid lessons** could deepen our mortgage pressure.
do: Ask two **schools** for posted role requirements and the college about a grant this winter.
Enroll only in an **accepted course** with grant fees, no lost lessons and partner pickup; otherwise wait next intake.
Apply in year one after **2031** if qualified and posted paid work covers travel, mortgage and childcare; keep pupils until offered.
feel: I feel **anxious** about recording income while I can check a funded route.
fieldNote: She values a **school credential** only if nearby schools accept it for paid work.
Her partner’s shifting **rota** makes course-night childcare a real gate alongside grant funding and paid lesson hours.
S3.quote: A degree in music is useful, yet it is not a school teaching license.

steps.text: Ask two schools for accepted teaching requirements and college for fee grant
Enrol only if course accepted, grant covers fees, partner covers pickup and paid lessons remain
Apply first year after 2031 only if qualified and posted pay covers travel, mortgage and childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our children AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to choose work carefully, with capable robot players around 2039. I would still ask what the next wedding pays before promising a new house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I could be a stronger teacher or still play weddings, but I cannot count on either income today. The mortgage and our thin savings remain real even with a long warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the six pupils and signed weddings this year, then move fifteen from each paid recording date into a separate reserve after the electricity arrears clear. In the first year after 2036, I’d renew a teaching room only if paid pupils cover rent and travel; I’d apply for a posted school music role only if my accepted qualification and its wage cover travel, the mortgage and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about today’s money rather than the calendar date. A decade helps me ask better questions, but it does not make this month’s payment smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the fifteen come from current bill money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fifteen is extra savings above our current thin account, not money already reserved for the mortgage. If the studio does not pay, there is nothing to transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let the children enjoy an instrument without telling them music must become their job. I want them to know both the joy and the actual fee.

I would still check **wedding fees** before thinking about robots around 2039.
think: At 53 I might still **teach or play**, but neither income is promised now.
Our **mortgage and thin savings** keep ordinary pressure on the household.
do: Keep six **pupils** and signed weddings; save fifteen from paid recordings only after arrears clear.
Renew a **teaching room** after 2036 only if paid pupils cover rent and travel.
Apply for a posted **school role** after 2036 only if qualified pay covers travel, mortgage and childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current bills despite a longer runway.
fieldNote: Her **baseline money worry** persists even though the 2036 clock allows planning.
The new **reserve transfer** follows paid recordings and cleared arrears; school work needs accepted credentials and wages.
S4.quote: A decade helps me ask better questions, but it does not make this month’s payment smaller.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because practice-track orders could stop before lessons replace them. Written studio orders, fair lender terms if cash falls short and a funded teaching credential schools accept would help me keep earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You might ask whether a music degree makes the mortgage easy. It does not. A paid date in the diary matters more to our lender than the name of my degree.

headlineQuote: A paid date in the diary matters more to our lender than the name of my degree.
portrait: At **43**, Daria is an experienced clarinet teacher and wedding player with a bachelor’s degree in music.
Her low **music pay**, partner’s variable catering hours and thin savings strain a household with two children and a mortgage.
She uses AI **occasionally** for calendars and considers school teaching only with an accepted funded credential.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens recorded practice tracks first, while capable robot players arrive around 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end practice-track orders before she replaces them with paid lessons.
whatWouldHelp: Written **studio dates**, fair lender terms if needed and an accepted funded teaching credential would help.
